{{short description|Dutch biologist and geneticist}}
'''Marjolein Kriek''' (born 22 November 1973)<ref name = onlinecv>[https://openaccess.leidenuniv.nl/bitstream/handle/1887/12479/Back.pdf?sequence=17 Online curriculum vitae, Leiden University]</ref> is a Dutch clinical geneticist at the [[Leiden University Medical Center]]. In 2008, at age 34, she became the first woman and probably the first European to have her total DNA genome sequenced.<ref name = Dulcinea>{{cite web | last = Coats | first = Christopher | title = Dr. Marjolein Kriek, First Woman to Have Her DNA Sequence Determined | date = December 27, 2009 | url = http://www.findingdulcinea.com/features/profiles/k/marjolein-kriek.html | accessdate = 3 January 2012 | archive-date = 13 August 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210813171219/http://www.findingdulcinea.com/features/profiles/k/marjolein-kriek.html | url-status = dead }}</ref><ref name = ScienceDaily>{{cite web | last = | first = | title = First Female DNA Sequenced | publisher = ScienceDaily | date = 26 May 2008 | url = https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2008/05/080526155300.htm | accessdate = }}</ref><ref name = Mina>{{cite web | last = | first = | title = Dutch Doctor is first woman to have DNA mapped | publisher = Mina | date = 1 June 2008 | url = http://macedoniaonline.eu/content/view/1652/56/ | accessdate = 3 January 2012}}</ref><ref name = Davies>{{cite book | last = Davies | first = Kevin | title = The $1,000 Genome: The Revolution in DNA Sequencing and the New Era of Personalized Medicine | publisher = Free Press | edition = 1st | location =  | year = 2010 | pages = [https://archive.org/details/1000genomerevolu0000davi/page/212 212–213] | isbn = 1-4165-6959-6 | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/1000genomerevolu0000davi/page/212 }}</ref>
[[Image:Statue of Marjolein Kriek (Q101023883) - 7.jpg|thumb|150px|right|Statue for  Marjolein Kriek, Nijmegen, the Netherlands. Detail of the computer print:[[Image:Statue for Marjolein Kriek by Bas van Vlijmen (detail), Toernooiveld, Nijmegen, the Netherlands.jpg|150px|right]]]]

==Sequencing project==
[[Leiden University]] announced the completion of the nine-month-long<ref name = Mina/> sequencing of Kriek's genome on 26 May 2008,<ref name = ScienceDaily/><ref name = Davies/> though the results of the study were published later. The study was initiated by Gert-Jan van Ommen of the LUMC team and director of the Center for Medical Systems Biology (CMSB), to gain insight in X-chromosome variability. The data set contained significant redundancy, as each base pair was sampled an average of seven to eight times.<ref name = ScienceDaily/><ref name = Davies/> The sequencing has been performed in close collaboration with a spin-off company, 'ServiceXS'. <ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.genomescan.nl |title=ServiceXS/ GenomeScan}}</ref>

At the time, Kriek was one of five or six people to have their entire genome sequenced, the others being [[James D. Watson]], [[Craig Venter]], two Yoruba men<ref name = Dulcinea/><ref name = ScienceDaily/> and possibly Dan Stoicescu of Switzerland.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/03/04/health/research/04geno.html |title=Gene Map Becomes a Luxury Item |work=The New York Times |date=2008-03-04 |accessdate=2010-02-24 |first=Amy |last=Harmon}}</ref>

==Career and research interests==
Kriek was born in [[Leiden]] and obtained her doctorate in Biomedical Science at Leiden University in 2002. Her graduate studies included [[Genetic screen|mutation screening]] in intellectually disabled people. Kriek's subsequent research interests similarly focussed on the diagnosis and clinical significance of genomic imbalances and  micro rearrangements as the causes of [[Developmental disability|developmental delay]], [[intellectual disability]] and [[Congenital disorder|congenital syndromes]].<ref name = onlinecv/>
